briefings.topic: AURA Strategic Planning Update and Three Proposed Study Areas
briefings.presenter_role: Executive Director, Arvada Urban Renewal Authority (AURA)
prose_paragraphs: AURA Executive Director Peri Prisco, joined by colleagues Alex Vanzante and Brien Hall, presented the results of AURA's ongoing strategic planning process and proposed three geographic areas that staff and the AURA board believe warrant deeper study as potential future urban renewal zones. Prisco framed the presentation around four strategic priorities that AURA has identified in alignment with the City Council's broader strategic plan: strategic alignment with city initiatives, supporting durable improvements, catalyzing private investment by addressing blighted conditions, and creating innovative place-making. She emphasized that the request was not for council to approve the creation of any urban renewal areas, but simply to endorse further study. She also noted that any new urban renewal work must comply with Colorado House Bill 15-1348, which expands AURA's board composition and adds negotiation requirements for Tax Increment Financing (TIF) in new project areas.

The three proposed study areas are distinct in character and timeline. The Arvada K-8 elementary and middle school site and the adjacent Ralston Road corridor represent the fastest-moving opportunity: Jefferson County School District has declared the K-8 school surplus, the City holds a right of first refusal, and Prisco estimated a study could produce an adopted area plan within nine to twelve months. The site sits adjacent to City Hall, Wolff Park, and Ralston Road, and the question raised was whether coordinated public investment could achieve broader civic outcomes — connectivity, public amenities, infrastructure — beyond what the private market would produce on its own. The Marshall Street corridor between Grandview and 52nd Avenue is an established employment area containing offices, light industrial, and some residential uses; AURA sees an opportunity to proactively manage how employment and residential uses coexist and to reduce barriers to reinvestment, with a study estimated at two to three years. The Squire Lake sub-area at the Sheridan/I-76 gateway is the most complex, with an estimated study timeline of three to five years; its primary challenge is the Ralston Creek and Clear Creek floodplains, which have historically fragmented infrastructure and limited development, and AURA's question is whether an urban renewal economic model could generate enough value to fund the large public infrastructure improvements the existing Squire Lake Sub-Area Plan envisions.

Council discussion surfaced several substantive concerns. Councilmember Ambrose pressed hard on anti-displacement protections, particularly for the Marshall Street corridor, which she identified as home to some of the city's most naturally occurring affordable housing; she noted that redevelopment pressure could spill over into unincorporated Adams County neighborhoods across Sheridan whose children attend Arvada schools. Multiple councilmembers expressed skepticism that urban renewal tools, in practice, tend to produce predominantly residential outcomes rather than preserving employment uses, citing prior experience along Ralston Road. Several councilmembers signaled a preference for prioritizing the Squire Lake sub-area, which one member described as a place where urban renewal is most clearly the right tool because infrastructure barriers are too large for the market to clear alone. There was also discussion of AURA's staff capacity to pursue all three areas simultaneously. Prisco indicated she would follow up individually with each councilmember to capture their input.

questions_raised: How has AURA historically managed demographic displacement and provided anti-displacement protections for residents in areas it has studied or redeveloped?

Given that the Marshall Street corridor contains some of Arvada's most affordable naturally-occurring housing, how will AURA ensure that commercial redevelopment does not indirectly displace residents in adjacent neighborhoods, including unincorporated Adams County?

In prior urban renewal projects along Ralston Road, commercial and employment uses largely gave way to residential development — how will AURA prevent the same outcome in Marshall Street, which is intended to preserve an employment center?
Does AURA have sufficient staff capacity to pursue all three study areas simultaneously, or should council prioritize one or two?
Should the Squire Lake sub-area be treated as the highest priority given the scale of infrastructure barriers and the existing community vision already documented in the Sub-Area Plan?

For the K-8 site, does the City need AURA as a tool at all, given the City already holds a right of first refusal — could the City simply secure the property and decide later whether to designate it an urban renewal area?
What is the timeline pressure on the K-8 site decision, given the school district's surplus declaration and competing buyer interest?
Does using AURA for the K-8 site give the City meaningful additional leverage over what gets built there, compared to acting through the right of first refusal alone?
What is the current status of the facilities master plan for the K-8 site and how will planned police/justice facility needs inform whether any portion of the site is available for redevelopment?
Is part of the Ralston Road corridor already within an existing AURA project area, and would a new K-8/Ralston study area overlap with or duplicate that coverage?
